name: Roman history
subtitle: 753 BCE to 476 CE
brief: SAMPLE · From a village on seven hills to the biggest empire of the ancient world.

lessons.heading: A village on seven hills
lessons.body:
*SAMPLE text for testing. Not reviewed.*

Rome began as a cluster of farming villages on hills beside the river Tiber, in central Italy. The Romans later told a founding story: twin brothers, Romulus and Remus, were left to die as babies, saved by a she-wolf and raised by a shepherd. As young men they quarrelled over where to build a city, and Romulus killed his brother. The city took his name. Roman writers dated this founding to 753 BCE. Historians treat the story as legend, but archaeology does show huts on the Palatine Hill from around that time.

## The age of kings

According to tradition, seven kings ruled early Rome. Some were Latin, some Sabine and the last few Etruscan. The Etruscans lived to the north and were skilled builders, metalworkers and traders. Under their influence Rome drained the marshy valley that became the Forum, built its first big temples and laid out its first paved streets.

The Romans remembered their last king, Tarquin the Proud, as a tyrant. In the traditional story his son attacked a noblewoman named Lucretia, and the nobles rose up and drove the royal family out. The usual date given is 509 BCE.

## A city without a king

After the kings, the Romans swore never to accept a single ruler again. The word for king, *rex*, became an insult in Roman politics for centuries. Instead they built a system where power was shared and limited in time. That system was the Republic, from the Latin *res publica*, meaning "the public thing".

Early Rome was small and often at war with its neighbours. It fought other Latin towns, the Etruscan city of Veii, and hill peoples such as the Samnites. Around 390 BCE a band of Gauls from the north sacked the city itself, a shock that Romans never forgot. Rome rebuilt and kept fighting.

What made Rome unusual was how it treated those it beat. Instead of only taking land, it often turned defeated towns into allies who sent soldiers to its armies. Some were given full or partial citizenship. Over time this web of alliances gave Rome more soldiers than any rival in Italy.

- By about 270 BCE Rome controlled most of the Italian peninsula.
- Its allies kept their own local leaders but followed Rome in war.
- Roads such as the Via Appia, begun in 312 BCE, tied the network together.

By then the village on the hills had become the strongest power in Italy, and it was starting to look across the sea.

lessons.heading: How the Republic worked
lessons.body:
*SAMPLE text for testing. Not reviewed.*

The Roman Republic had no single written constitution. It ran on a mix of laws, customs and the respect people gave to tradition, which Romans called *mos maiorum*, "the way of the ancestors". Three parts mattered most: the magistrates, the Senate and the assemblies.

## Two consuls at the top

Each year the citizens elected two consuls. They commanded the armies and led the government, but each could block the other, and both left office after twelve months. Below them were other elected officials: praetors who ran the courts, quaestors who handled money, and aediles who looked after streets, markets and public games. In an emergency the Senate could ask for a dictator, a single leader with full power for at most six months.

## The Senate

The Senate was a council of former officials, a few hundred men who usually sat for life. In theory it only gave advice. In practice its advice was hard to ignore. It managed foreign affairs, the treasury and the provinces, and its members came mostly from rich, old families.

## The people

Ordinary citizens voted in assemblies that elected officials, passed laws and decided on war and peace. Votes were counted by groups, not by heads, and the groups were arranged so that the wealthy usually had more weight.

Early Roman society was split between patricians, a small group of noble families, and plebeians, everyone else. For about two hundred years the plebeians pushed for a fairer share of power in what historians call the Conflict of the Orders. Their main tool was the threat to walk out of the city and refuse to fight.

They won real gains:

- Tribunes of the plebs, officials who could veto actions that harmed ordinary citizens.
- The Twelve Tables, around 450 BCE, which put the main laws in writing so everyone could see them.
- The right for plebeians to become consul, from 367 BCE onwards.

## Why it lasted

The Republic's balance of short terms, shared offices and the power to block worked well for a small city. Ambitious men competed for glory inside the rules, and the system rewarded service in war. Problems came later, when Rome grew huge and a few commanders gained more money and more soldiers than the old system could control.

lessons.heading: Rome against Carthage
lessons.body:
*SAMPLE text for testing. Not reviewed.*

Carthage was a rich trading city on the coast of North Africa, in what is now Tunisia. It had been founded by Phoenician settlers and ruled a sea empire that stretched across the western Mediterranean. As Rome finished taking Italy, the two powers met in Sicily. Between 264 and 146 BCE they fought three wars, called the Punic Wars after the Latin name for the Phoenicians.

## The First Punic War

The first war, from 264 to 241 BCE, was fought mostly at sea. Rome had almost no navy at the start. It built fleets quickly and fitted its ships with a boarding bridge, the *corvus*, so that sea battles could be fought like land battles. Rome lost many ships to storms but kept building. It won, and took Sicily as its first province outside Italy.

## Hannibal

The second war, from 218 to 201 BCE, is the most famous. The Carthaginian general Hannibal marched an army from Spain over the Pyrenees and the Alps into Italy, bringing war elephants with him. Many of the elephants and men died on the way.

Once in Italy, Hannibal beat Roman armies again and again. At Cannae in 216 BCE he surrounded a much larger Roman force and destroyed it. It was one of the worst defeats in Roman history. Yet Rome refused to make peace. Most of its Italian allies stayed loyal, and Rome avoided big battles while it rebuilt its strength.

## Scipio turns the war

A young Roman general, Publius Cornelius Scipio, took the war to Spain and then to Africa itself. Carthage called Hannibal home to defend the city. At Zama in 202 BCE Scipio defeated him, and he earned the name Africanus. Carthage gave up its fleet and its lands outside Africa, and paid heavy sums to Rome for decades.

## The end of Carthage

Fifty years later, some Roman senators still saw Carthage as a danger. The senator Cato the Elder is said to have ended his speeches by calling for its destruction. The third war, from 149 to 146 BCE, ended with Roman soldiers burning the city and enslaving its people. In the same year, Rome also destroyed the Greek city of Corinth.

- Rome now ruled Sicily, Sardinia, much of Spain and North Africa.
- Wealth and enslaved people flowed into Italy.
- Rome had become the strongest power in the Mediterranean.

lessons.heading: Why the Republic fell
lessons.body:
*SAMPLE text for testing. Not reviewed.*

Rome's victories made it rich, but the riches were spread unevenly. Wealthy families bought up land and worked it with enslaved people taken in war. Many small farmers, who had served for years in the army, came home to find they could not compete. They drifted to the city of Rome, poor and angry. Politics turned rough.

## The Gracchi brothers

In 133 BCE the tribune Tiberius Gracchus proposed giving public land to poor citizens. Senators who opposed him clubbed him to death in the street. His younger brother Gaius pushed further reforms and was also killed, in 121 BCE. For the first time in centuries, Roman politics had been settled by violence, and it would happen again.

## Armies with their own loyalty

For centuries, Roman soldiers were citizens who owned property and went home after a war. Around 107 BCE the general Gaius Marius began recruiting poor men who had nothing to go home to. They looked to their general, not to the Senate, for pay and for land when they retired. Generals now had armies that were loyal to them.

The general Sulla was the first to use such an army against Rome itself. He marched on the city in 88 BCE and later made himself dictator, killing many of his enemies.

## Caesar crosses the line

Julius Caesar conquered Gaul between 58 and 50 BCE and became hugely popular with his soldiers and the people. The Senate ordered him to give up his army. In 49 BCE he led it over the Rubicon, a small river that marked the edge of his province. Doing that was treason. He won the civil war that followed and was made dictator for life.

On the Ides of March, 15 March 44 BCE, a group of senators stabbed him to death at a meeting of the Senate. They hoped to bring back the old Republic.

## One man in charge

Instead another civil war began. Caesar's adopted heir Octavian defeated Mark Antony and Cleopatra at the naval battle of Actium in 31 BCE. In 27 BCE the Senate gave Octavian the name Augustus. He kept the old offices, and the Senate still met, but real power sat with him and his army. The Republic was over. Rome had its first emperor, though Augustus preferred to be called *princeps*, "first citizen".

lessons.heading: Life in the empire
lessons.body:
*SAMPLE text for testing. Not reviewed.*

For about two hundred years after Augustus, the empire was mostly at peace inside its borders. Romans called this the *Pax Romana*, the Roman peace. At its largest, under the emperor Trajan around 117 CE, the empire stretched from Britain to Egypt and from Spain to the river Euphrates. Perhaps 50 to 70 million people lived inside it.

## Roads, water and concrete

The Romans were outstanding engineers. They built about 80,000 kilometres of paved roads, so that armies, officials and traders could move quickly. Aqueducts carried fresh water for many kilometres into cities, feeding public fountains, baths and toilets.

![](roman-history.i04)

Roman concrete, made with volcanic ash, was strong and lasted for centuries. Some harbour walls built with it still stand in the sea today. It also made huge domes possible, such as the Pantheon in Rome, still the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world.

## Cities and games

Life centred on cities. A Roman town usually had a forum for business and politics, temples, a bath house and often a theatre or arena. In Rome itself the Colosseum, opened in 80 CE, held around 50,000 people. Crowds watched gladiator fights, animal hunts and public executions there. Chariot races at the Circus Maximus drew even bigger crowds.

## One language, many peoples

Latin was the language of government and the army in the west, while Greek stayed the common language in the east. Local languages and gods carried on, and the Romans often added foreign gods to their own. Citizenship spread step by step until, in 212 CE, the emperor Caracalla gave it to almost all free men in the empire.

Not everyone shared in the good life. A large share of people were enslaved, and many free people were very poor. Women could not vote or hold office, although some rich women owned property and ran businesses.

## Guarding the edges

The army, about 300,000 soldiers at its peak, guarded long frontiers. In northern Britain the emperor Hadrian had a wall built from coast to coast, begun in 122 CE. It ran about 73 miles, or 117 kilometres. Along the Rhine and the Danube rivers, forts and watchtowers marked where Roman control ended.

lessons.heading: The fall in the west
lessons.body:
*SAMPLE text for testing. Not reviewed.*

In the third century CE the empire came close to breaking apart. Between 235 and 284 CE more than twenty men claimed the throne, and most of them were killed. Armies fought each other, the money lost its value, plague spread, and enemies crossed the borders. Historians call this the Crisis of the Third Century.

## Splitting the work

The emperor Diocletian, who came to power in 284 CE, decided the empire was too big for one ruler. He shared power with three others, two senior emperors and two juniors, each in charge of a region. He also reorganised taxes and the army.

Constantine the Great later reunited the empire under his own rule. He supported Christianity, which had often been persecuted, and in 330 CE he made the old Greek city of Byzantium his new capital. It was renamed Constantinople, today's Istanbul. In 380 CE Christianity became the official religion of the empire.

After the emperor Theodosius died in 395 CE, the empire was divided for good into a western half and an eastern half, each with its own emperor.

## Pressure on the borders

In the late fourth century, groups such as the Goths, Vandals and Franks moved into Roman lands, some pushed west by the Huns. Some came as allies or hired soldiers, others as invaders. In 410 CE the Visigoths sacked the city of Rome, the first time in eight hundred years that a foreign enemy had taken it. The Vandals sacked it again in 455 CE.

## The last western emperor

In 476 CE a Germanic general named Odoacer removed the teenage emperor Romulus Augustulus and did not bother to name a new one. That date is usually given as the end of the Western Roman Empire. By then the west had already broken into kingdoms run by new rulers, though many of them kept Roman laws, Latin and the church.

## Rome did not end everywhere

The eastern half, which historians call the Byzantine Empire, lasted for almost another thousand years. Its people still called themselves Romans. It fell only when the Ottoman sultan Mehmed II captured Constantinople in 1453.

Why the west fell is still debated. Common explanations include:

- Civil wars that weakened the army and the treasury.
- Pressure from migrating peoples on long frontiers.
- An economy and tax system under heavy strain.

Most historians now see a slow change over many years rather than one sudden collapse.

quiz.prompt: [SAMPLE] Who was the first Roman emperor?
quiz.explanation: Octavian took the name Augustus in 27 BCE.

quiz.prompt: [SAMPLE] Which city did Rome fight in the Punic Wars?
quiz.explanation: Carthage, in North Africa, was destroyed in 146 BCE.

quiz.prompt: [SAMPLE] What was the Colosseum mainly used for?
quiz.explanation: It held about 50,000 people for games and shows.

quiz.prompt: [SAMPLE] In which year did Julius Caesar die?
quiz.explanation: He was stabbed on the Ides of March, 15 March 44 BCE.

quiz.prompt: [SAMPLE] Which language did Roman government and the army use in the west?
quiz.explanation: Latin. Italian grew out of it much later.

quiz.prompt: [SAMPLE] Which wall marked the north of Roman Britain?
quiz.explanation: Hadrian's Wall ran about 73 miles across northern England.

quiz.prompt: [SAMPLE] What could a tribune of the plebs do?
options: Veto actions that harmed ordinary citizens
quiz.explanation: Tribunes could block actions that harmed ordinary citizens.

quiz.prompt: [SAMPLE] Where did Hannibal surround and destroy a larger Roman army in 216 BCE?
quiz.explanation: Cannae was one of the worst defeats in Roman history.

quiz.prompt: [SAMPLE] Which general began recruiting poor men with no property into the army?
quiz.explanation: Around 107 BCE Marius recruited men who looked to their general for pay and land.

quiz.prompt: [SAMPLE] Who removed the last western Roman emperor in 476 CE?
quiz.explanation: Odoacer removed Romulus Augustulus and named no one in his place.
